cycle.name: New 6-week cycle
focus: Power snatches move from doubles to triples
Saturday HYROX run → station → run experiment
cycle.full_text:
This week felt a little different in New York.

Friday marked 25 years since September 11, and there are certain days when this enormous city somehow feels very small. A day to remember the people we lost, the people who ran toward danger, and the resilience and very particular kind of community that has defined New York in the years since.

Showing up for one another feels like a pretty good note to carry into a new week.

And because New York contains multitudes, the city also spent the week absolutely losing its mind over tennis. The US Open has been chaos in the best possible way—five-hour matches, huge upsets, an all-American men's semifinal, and Ben Shelton casually knocking out Carlos Alcaraz at 3:33 IN THE MORNING with a 146-mph ace. Apparently nobody in Queens believes in bedtime.

Meanwhile, back inside CFNYC, we have our own little athletic dramas unfolding.

CrossFit heads into Week 2 of our new cycle: more power snatch reps, another date with cluster squats, continued pulling practice, and a Saturday HYROX session that would very much like to know how well you can run after doing race-volume stations.

ATHX is firmly in fall race-prep territory, practicing the very useful skill of moving between strength, endurance and MetCon without losing the plot. And Strength rolls into Week 7 with heavy triples—squat Monday, bench Thursday—while Oly puts the clean, push press and jerk together.

Some of us are starting new cycles. Some are deep into them. Some are getting ready to race. Everyone is building toward something.

Come train. Learn something. Cheer for somebody. Add another good rep to the pile.

Let's have a week.

crossfit.name: CrossFit
crossfit.note: Week 2 of 6: more power snatch reps, another date with cluster squats, continued pulling practice, and a Saturday HYROX session testing how well you run after race-volume stations.

mon.title: Power snatch triples + 8 rounds for time

sections.label: Strength
lines: A1. Power Snatch — 4 sets of 3, building
A2. Feet-Elevated Parallette Push Up — 4 sets of 8–12

mon.coach_notes:
Week 2 means our power snatches go from doubles to triples. It's only one extra rep, but that extra rep asks you to maintain the same speed and positions for a little longer. The goal is still power—three crisp reps, not two beautiful snatches followed by one barbell-related negotiation.

Then we have eight rounds where small sets are sneaky. Nothing here looks particularly intimidating on its own, which means the temptation is to come out very hot. But this is meant to stay aerobic and continuously moving for roughly 10–12 minutes for most of us.

Choose a deadlift you can keep unbroken—or 3/2 when needed—and scale the push-ups so seven doesn't slowly become a three-act production. The double unders should feel like a quick reset before you pick the bar back up.

The goal isn't huge bursts of effort. It's tiny amounts of work with almost no wasted time between them.

tue.title: Cluster back squat + 2 × 4-min AMRAP

sections.label: Strength
lines: A. Cluster Back Squat — 5 sets of 2-2-1, building
B. Pendlay Row — 3 sets of 8 across, then 1 max-effort set with 20% less

tue.coach_notes:
Cluster squats, round two. Same 2-2-1 structure as last week, another opportunity to get comfortable using those little intra-set rests to reset your brace and keep the quality of all five reps high.

Then Pendlay rows get a fun little twist: three sets of eight across, followed by a max-effort set with 20% less weight. Think of it as heavy work first, then a lighter back-off set that lets us accumulate more quality pulling volume after the hard stuff is done.

And then we race the clock.

The row is where you score, so the first 30 reps are essentially your buy-in. Ideally, you're arriving at the erg with 1:30–2:00 to actually work.

That means your scaling matters. Hang squat cleans should be unbroken or 8/7; pull-ups can comfortably be 5/5/5. If either movement turns into extended staring, we have accidentally made a different workout.

Get through the work efficiently, then make the rower regret meeting you.

wed.title: One long list, for time (HYROX-style)
wed.coach_notes:
Today is one long, glorious list.

There is no complicated strategy here—but there is a very important one: do not confuse "for time" with "as fast as humanly possible from rep one."

Long efforts reward athletes who understand sustainable output. Your aerobic system is doing the heavy lifting here, and the goal is to keep producing work without accumulating so much fatigue at any one station that you need a congressional recess before moving on.

So break things before they break you. Keep transitions purposeful. Let the machines settle you rather than destroy you. And remember that there are 50 wall balls waiting at the very end, quietly minding their business while you make decisions they will eventually hold you accountable for.

This one is less about winning a station and more about never really stopping.

A very long list. One item at a time. See you on the other side.

thu.title: RDL + pull skill, partner 14 rounds

sections.label: Strength
lines: A1. Romanian Deadlift — 4 sets of 6–8, building
A2. Pull-up / C2B / Bar Muscle-Up Practice — 4 sets

sections.label: Partner Conditioning
lines: 14 Rounds For Time (alternate rounds with a partner):

thu.coach_notes:
We're back to Romanian deadlifts + pulling skill practice to start. Keep building those RDLs while owning the hinge, then use your four pulling sets for your current project: kipping mechanics, pull-ups, chest-to-bar, transitions, or full bar muscle-ups.

Then grab a friend. This is classic you-go-I-go conditioning, which changes the game a little. Your partner's working minute becomes your recovery minute, meaning you have permission to push considerably harder than you would if you were responsible for all 14 rounds yourself.

Aim for roughly one minute per round. Move hard, tag out, then actually recover: breathe, shake out your arms, and get ready to go again.

And because friendship apparently wasn't competitive enough already, you are now directly responsible for how long your partner gets to rest. Choose wisely.

fri.title: Tempo cyclist squat + strict press, 15-min AMRAP

sections.label: Strength
lines: A1. Goblet Cyclist Squat — 3 sets of 10–12 @ 31X1 tempo
A2. Strict Press — 3 sets of 8–10, building

fri.coach_notes:
We start with another week of tempo cyclist squats + strict press. That 31X1 tempo is still asking you to own three slow seconds down and the bottom position before standing with intent. If last week helped you find the right loading, this week is your chance to make those same positions stronger.

Then:

The front squat is heavy enough to demand respect, but the real story today is gymnastics sustainability.

Six HSPU and nine toes-to-bar are very manageable numbers...until you've encountered them six or seven times. Your best strategy may be 3/3 on the wall or 5/4 on the bar from the beginning, rather than proving you can go unbroken early and discovering several rounds later that you no longer can.

Around two minutes per round is a great early target. The challenge is seeing how long you can keep that clockwork going as shoulders, grip and midline fatigue start negotiating new terms.

You don't need to win minute two. You need to still be moving in minute fourteen.

sat.title: 4 × (run → station → run) with 3-min rests

sections.label: Conditioning
lines: 500m run · 50m Sled push (Open 5/3, Pro 7/5) · 1000m run · Rest 3 min
500m run · 80m Sandbag walking lunge (20/10 kg) · 1000m run · Rest 3 min

sat.coach_notes:
Today we're running a little experiment.

Four times, you'll run 500m → complete a mostly race-volume station → run 1,000m, with three minutes of recovery before doing it all over again.

This is a chance to learn something incredibly useful for race day: what happens to your running when a station gets involved?

We want you pushing these pieces hard. The first 500m shows us what you can produce going into the station. That second 1,000m asks whether you can find your running again when your legs, lungs, or both have recently been occupied elsewhere.

Pay attention to how each station changes you. Heavy sled legs don't feel like post-row legs. Lunges create a different problem than wall balls. Learning how quickly you can settle back into a productive run is part of becoming a better hybrid athlete—not waiting until you feel recovered, but learning to recover while moving.

You get three minutes between pieces, so these aren't meant to be cautious little efforts.

Push. Learn. Recover. Repeat.

announcements.title: Halloween Throwdown — last weekend of October
announcements.detail: In-house partner competition (pairs; women's, men's, mixed divisions), morning session. Costumes encouraged; Best Costume award. Exact date, time and registration coming.
announcements.full_text:
🎃 CFNYC HALLOWEEN THROWDOWN

Remember when we said putting this in the newsletter made it legally binding? Well, we're committed now.

This Halloween season, we're throwing a CFNYC In-House Partner Competition—and we now have a few more details to share.

We're aiming for the last weekend of October, in the morning, so you can throw down with your gym friends, take some ridiculous photos, and still have plenty of time to go home, recover, and transform into a person who definitely did not spend their morning doing CrossFit.

Exact date + time are coming soon. But here's what we do know:

Teams will be pairs of two, competing in women's, men's, or mixed divisions. The workouts will have prescribed weights and standards for each division, so grab the person whose particular brand of fitness complements yours and start forming alliances now.

And, obviously, costumes are highly encouraged.

There will be workouts. There will be prizes. There will be bragging rights. And there will absolutely be a Best Costume award, because athletic performance matters, but so does committing aggressively to a theme.

Come compete. Come cheer. Come hang out. Whether you're trying to win the whole thing or simply trying to convince your partner that your two-person costume concept is worth doing burpees in, we want you there.

For now: keep the last weekend of October open. Find your partner. Start plotting your costume.

Exact date, time, registration details, workouts, and everything else are coming.

Fitness will be judged. Costumes will be judged. Commitment to the bit will be rewarded.

announcements.title: 2027 CrossFit Open dates
announcements.detail: 27.1 Feb 18 · 27.2 Feb 25 · 27.3 Mar 4. Pick a thing to work on between now and February and tell your coaches.
announcements.full_text:
👀 THE OPEN IS COMING. LET'S BUILD SOMETHING.

We know February feels approximately 400 years away. It is not.

The 2027 CrossFit Open dates are officially on the calendar:

27.1 — February 18
27.2 — February 25
27.3 — March 4

And this year, we want CFNYC IN.

Not because we expect everyone to suddenly become a competitive CrossFit athlete. The Open is three weeks where the thing we do together all year gets a start line, a scorecard, and a whole lot more cheering.

It's also one of the best fitness check-ins we get. Do it year after year and suddenly you have actual data: Am I stronger? Is my engine better? Did the movement that stopped me last year become something I can do now? CrossFit specifically uses the Open as an annual benchmark for exactly that kind of progress.

So between now and February, pick a thing.

Maybe it's your first pull-up. Double unders. Toes-to-bar. Getting stronger with a barbell. Learning to pace instead of seeing God four minutes into an AMRAP.

Tell your coaches. Let us help you work on it.

Then, come February, we get to put all that training to use together.

Three workouts. Three weeks. One very loud CFNYC.

More Open hype incoming. Consider yourselves warned.

Fill out the interest form via the link in the newsletter.

announcements.title: Fall race season roll call
announcements.detail: Racing this fall (marathon, half, HYROX, ATHX, trail)? Tell your coaches or the Front Desk so the gym can show up and cheer.
announcements.full_text:
FALL RACE SEASON IS ON 🏁

The weather is about to get cooler, the training is getting suspiciously specific, and fall race season is officially upon us.

Marathons. Half marathons. HYROX. ATHX. Trail races. That slightly unhinged event your friend convinced you to sign up for six months ago and you are now realizing is, in fact, happening.

We want to know what you're doing.

One of our favorite things about CFNYC is that the fitness you build here goes out into the world with you—and we want to celebrate the hell out of it. We want to know what you're training for, when you're racing, where you're racing, and yes, we would very much like the opportunity to show up with signs and yell your name at an unreasonable volume.

So if you have anything on the calendar this fall, TELL US. Tell your coaches, email the Front Desk, send us the details. Big race, first race, 47th race, something completely outside your comfort zone—we want all of it.

Because PRs are cool. Watching your gym friends do hard things out in the wild is cooler.

CFNYC race season roll call: what are we training for?!
